newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's North Sea oil policy creates few waves.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's North Sea oil policy creates few waves.

text.p: Britain's booming oil and gas industry is relaxed about energy policy under a future Labour government but fears rising costs from planned social legislation.

Labour, out of power since 1979 but favourite to win Thursday's general election, has shed its high tax image and is not about to surprise companies making record profits from Britain's abundant hydrocarbon reserves.
"We've said quite clearly there will be no shock taxes in the North Sea," Labour's energy spokesman John Battle told Reuters.
Labour has promised a one-off levy on the windfall profits of utilities privatised by the Conservative government, including gas and electricity companies.
Britain's oil and gas industry is reliving the heady days of the 1980s, with production and development running at record levels and tax receipts rising.
Government figures released on Monday showed oil and gas companies trading profits jumped 30 percent to 14.4 billion sterling in 1996.
Tax revenue also rose sharply to 3.6 billion pounds but remains dwarfed by receipts of 10-11 billion pounds a year during Britain's first oil boom in the mid-1980s.

While some industry sources claim there is room for a tightening of the North Sea fiscal regime -- widely seen as the most generous in the world -- most argue against any change which could divert investment to Latin America or North Africa where exploration is also burgeoning.

"Anything which rocks the boat could have a very significant adverse effect," said Andrew Searle, government and public affairs director at the UK Offshore Operators Association (UKOOA), which groups 34 companies operating in British waters.

"Competition globally is hotting up against a background of a price of oil which is still very low... If they (Labour) keep more or less what's in place at the moment then I think the industry would be reasonably happy," Searle said.

The impact of proposals to alter North Sea licensing regulations to encourage development of fallow oil and gas deposits, including tighter deadlines for exploration activity, would have only a marginal impact, industry sources said.
By contrast, Labour's plans for employment and social legislation are causing concern among UKOOA's members.
"There's a whole raft of social legislation we are very worried about in terms of the impact it may have on raising the industry's costs," said UKOOA's Searle.
Searle said Labour's commitment to signing the European Union Social Chapter and the possibility of compulsory trade union recognition could damage the industry's rosy prospects.
EU attempts to regulate working hours, if applied to the offshore oil and gas industry, could also have a serious impact, he said.
Labour would consult widely on whether to oppose the introduction of a maximum 48-hour week in the North Sea, balancing competing health and safety arguments.

"The most dangerous part of the oil industry is actually the helicopter journeys to and from the rigs so if you increase them you increase the risk and that's got to be taken into consideration," said Battle.

Another priority for an incoming Labour energy minister would be completion of domestic gas market deregulation, already piloted in the southwest of England, but Battle would not be tied to the timetable set by the Conservative government last month.
"We're not interested in slowing down competition but ... what's starting to worry us is that the lessons of the southwest have not yet been learnt in terms of consumers' rights," said Battle.
